title: Can you tell someone is sick just by looking at their face?
blurb: Scientists showed children photos of the same people when ill and when well. By age 8 or 9, most children could spot the sick face.

cover.alt: Pairs of photos of the same person, once when ill and once when well, used in the doctor game and the dinner game.
cover.credit: Figure 1, Leung et al., Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: Infection Detection: Children Avoid Sick Faces
source.authors: Tiffany S. Leung, Guangyu Zeng, Sarah E. Maylott, Shantalle N. Martinez, Krisztina V. Jakobsen and Elizabeth A. Simpson

original.title: Infection detection in faces: children's development of pathogen avoidance
original.authors: Leung, T. S., Zeng, G., Maylott, S. E., Martinez, S. N., Jakobsen, K. V., and Simpson, E. A.

cards.b: Germs can pass from a sick person to you if you get too close. Grown-ups can often tell someone is ill just by looking at their face. Can children do this too? And at what age do children start to keep away from people who look sick?

Tiffany Leung, Elizabeth Simpson and their team study how babies and children learn about other people. Faces are a big part of that. They worked in the Social Cognition Lab at the University of Miami in the United States. They published this study in 2024.

22 people photographed their face while ill with a cold, flu or COVID-19. Later, each took another photo when well. The team showed the two photos of one person side by side to young children, older children and adults, and called them twins. In the doctor game, they asked which twin was sick. In the dinner game, they asked which twin to sit next to.

img.alt: Pairs of photos of the same person, once when ill and once when well, used in the doctor game and the dinner game.
img.credit: Figure 1, Leung et al., Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Just guessing is right half the time. In the doctor game, 8 to 9-year-olds were right 63 times out of 100, and adults 75 times. In the dinner game, both groups mostly chose the healthy twin. Most 4 to 5-year-olds were close to guessing. But a few were very good, and one young child beat every adult.

img.alt: Two graphs of scores for young children, older children and adults, with a dotted line at the score you would get by guessing.
img.credit: Figure 2, Leung et al., Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: This study used photos, not real people, and only 22 faces. It shows the skill grows with age, but not exactly why. Maybe older children know more about germs. Maybe they understand other people better. Earlier studies with pretend sick people found something similar: older children kept away more than younger ones.

Staying a little apart from sick people helps stop germs spreading. Many young children cannot yet spot sickness, so parents and older brothers and sisters can help them. Washing hands before eating and not sharing drinks also keep germs away. You can still wave hello to a sick friend from a little distance.

Play the doctor game yourselves. The photos with this card show the same people twice. One row shows them when healthy, and the other row when sick. Guess which row is sick, and say why. Tired eyes? A red nose? A frown? Everyone in the family should guess before you read on. The sick faces are in the bottom row.

img.alt: Two rows of face photos of the same people: the top row when healthy and the bottom row when sick.
img.credit: Figure 3, Leung et al., Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Your body gives you a 'yuck' feeling near things that might make you ill. That feeling can protect you. But it can also make someone who is ill feel left out and lonely. How can you keep safe from germs and still be kind to a friend who is sick?

when germs get into the body and make it unwell
keeping away from people or things that might make you ill

correct, or close to the right answer
